steps.text: Step 1: Cut out the helicopter — Cut along the dashed lines of the template; if using plain paper, sketch the solid and dashed guide lines then cut.
Step 2: Fold along the solid lines — Fold propeller blades A and B in opposite directions; fold X and Y panels toward center and fold Z upward to form the body and lower center of gravity.
Step 3: Do a test flight — Hold the helicopter by its body, raise it as high as you can, and drop it; observe blade rotation and performance changes when dropped from higher spots.
Step 4: Compare — Drop an unfolded paper the same size and a wadded paper ball together with the helicopter to compare fall rates and discuss air resistance.
Step 5: Experiment — Make one change (e.g., fold the bottom up, shorten or change blade shape) and observe how performance changes.
Step 6: Make a new model — Build additional versions (different paper, sizes) to test which sizes or materials work best.
Step 7: Reverse it — Note which direction the blades turn and identify a single change that will make them spin the opposite direction.
Step 8: Count the rotations — Measure shoulder height, drop the best-performing helicopter from shoulder height, and count rotations; use video or attach a ribbon if counting is difficult.
Step 9: Repeat — Repeat measuring, dropping, and counting from a lower height to compare results.
Step 10: Predict — Measure a taller height, predict rotations for that height, and record your prediction.
Step 11: Test your prediction — Drop from the taller height and compare results to the prediction; try other heights to improve predictions.

substitutions.alternative: Use a ruler, meter stick, a known-height object (e.g., step height or door frame) or a smartphone with a measuring app to estimate shoulder height
substitutions.conditions: Only use these substitutions for informal height/rotation counts. A ruler or meter stick must be long enough for the chosen drop height; using a smartphone app or estimating from known object heights may reduce measurement precision compared to a measuring tape.

substitutions.conditions: Knife use introduces safety risks and requires supervision; tearing may reduce accuracy of cut lines and affect flight. These are untested suggestions and are not from the source.

substitutions.alternative: Use a smartphone camera for recording/counting rotations (the source lists this as an optional alternative).
substitutions.conditions: Using the smartphone camera is appropriate for counting rotations; it does not replace ribbon if you planned to attach a ribbon for visibility.
